title: GCF & LCM
subtitle: Factors, Multiples, Distributing
bounds: PROTOCOL §4a, tightened. Every hidden × or ÷ is a times-table fact with both factors 2 to 10. T1: numbers ≤ 100 (factor-count numbers ≤ 36, primes ≤ 47). T2/T4/T5 GCF pairs: a = g × p, b = g × q with g, p, q ≤ 10 (p, q share no factor), so a, b ≤ 100. T3/T5 LCM operands 2 to 10 (6.NS.B.4 allows to 12; kept to 10 for §4a) with LCM ≤ 60. Correct answers ≤ 100; wrong choices ≤ 999. No two choices equal in value.

tiers.name: Factors & Primes
tiers.description: Factors, multiples, primes, and counting factors.

tiers.name: Greatest Common Factor
tiers.description: Find the GCF of two numbers up to 100.

tiers.name: Least Common Multiple
tiers.description: Find the LCM of two or three small numbers.

tiers.name: Factor Out the GCF
tiers.description: Write a sum as the GCF times a sum: 18 + 24 = 6(3 + 4).

tiers.name: GCF or LCM?
tiers.description: Story problems: pick the right tool, then use it.

MULTIPLE_FOR_FACTOR.student: That's a multiple. A factor divides the number evenly, so it's not bigger.
MULTIPLE_FOR_FACTOR.teacher: Picks a multiple of n when asked for a factor of n.

FACTOR_FOR_MULTIPLE.student: That's a factor. A multiple is the number times 1, 2, 3, and so on.
FACTOR_FOR_MULTIPLE.teacher: Picks a factor of m when asked for a multiple of m.

SHARES_FACTOR.student: Sharing a factor isn't enough. The division must come out even.
SHARES_FACTOR.teacher: Accepts a number that shares a factor with n (both even) as a factor or multiple of n.

SAME_LAST_DIGIT.student: Ending in the same digit doesn't make a multiple. Skip-count to check.
SAME_LAST_DIGIT.teacher: Thinks multiples of m end in m's digit (17 for 7, 26 for 6).

ODD_IS_PRIME.student: Odd isn't the same as prime. Try 3, 5, 7: does one divide it?

ONE_IS_PRIME.student: 1 is not prime. A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.

FORGOT_ONE_AND_SELF.student: Count 1 and the number itself too. They are factors.
FORGOT_ONE_AND_SELF.teacher: Leaves 1 and n out of n's factor count.

PAIRS_ONLY.student: Each factor pair gives two factors. Count every number, not the pairs.
PAIRS_ONLY.teacher: Counts factor pairs instead of factors.

SQUARE_TWICE.student: In 6 × 6 the 6 is one factor. Don't count it twice.
SQUARE_TWICE.teacher: Counts the square root of a perfect square twice.

LCM_FOR_GCF.student: That's a common multiple. The GCF divides both numbers, so it's small.
LCM_FOR_GCF.teacher: Gives the LCM when asked for the GCF.

NOT_GREATEST.student: That's a common factor, but not the greatest. Look for a bigger one.
NOT_GREATEST.teacher: Stops at a common factor smaller than the GCF.

SMALLER_NUMBER.student: The smaller number must divide the bigger one to be the GCF. It doesn't.
SMALLER_NUMBER.teacher: Gives the smaller number as the GCF when it does not divide the larger.

PRODUCT.student: a × b is a common multiple, but maybe not the least. Skip-count to check.
PRODUCT.teacher: Gives the product as the LCM when the numbers share a factor.

GCF_FOR_LCM.student: That's the GCF. The LCM is a multiple of both, so it's at least as big.
GCF_FOR_LCM.teacher: Gives the GCF when asked for the LCM.

LARGER_NUMBER.student: The bigger number isn't a multiple of the other. Keep skip-counting.
LARGER_NUMBER.teacher: Gives the larger number as the LCM when the smaller does not divide it.

NOT_LEAST.student: That's a common multiple, but not the least. A smaller one works.
NOT_LEAST.teacher: Gives a common multiple larger than the LCM.

SUBTRACTED_GCF.student: Divide each number by the GCF. Don't subtract it.
SUBTRACTED_GCF.teacher: Subtracts the GCF from each addend instead of dividing: 18 + 24 = 6(12 + 18).

ONE_TERM.student: Divide BOTH numbers by the GCF, not just one.
ONE_TERM.teacher: Divides only one addend by the GCF: 18 + 24 = 6(3 + 24).

WRONG_TOOL.student: Sharing into equal groups: GCF. Matching up or meeting again: LCM.
WRONG_TOOL.teacher: Uses GCF for an LCM situation or LCM for a GCF situation.

items.prompt: 60 red, 70 blue beads. Most identical bags, none left?
items.explanation: Equal sharing needs a common factor of 60 and 70. 60 = 10 × 6, 70 = 10 × 7: GCF 10.

items.prompt: 21 boys, 9 girls in identical teams. Most teams?
items.explanation: Equal sharing needs a common factor of 21 and 9. 21 = 3 × 7, 9 = 3 × 3: GCF 3.
